question: A 2-year-old girl presents to the emergency department with a 3-minute episode of a tonic-clonic seizure. The parents deny any previous history of seizure involving the patient or the family. Physical examination reveals an afebrile, well-groomed, and playful appearance, with normal vital signs. The patient carries a pink birthmark on the right side of her face extending from the forehead to the zygomatic arch. Which of the following findings is most likely on a head CT of this patient?

enhanced_information: The 2-year-old girl with a tonic-clonic seizure and a facial pink birthmark is suggestive of Sturge-Weber syndrome, a neurocutaneous disorder associated with facial capillary malformations and leptomeningeal angiomas. This condition can lead to cortical malformations and is known to cause seizures. Head CT findings in Sturge-Weber syndrome typically reveal prominent intraparenchymal white matter calcifications, particularly in the region corresponding to the affected vascular malformation. Therefore, the most likely finding on a head CT for this patient is prominent intraparenchymal white matter calcification, aligning with the consensus on the association between Sturge-Weber syndrome and seizure activity.
analysis: The clinical presentation of the 2-year-old girl, including the tonic-clonic seizure and the facial pink birthmark, is highly suggestive of Sturge-Weber syndrome. This neurocutaneous disorder is characterized by facial capillary malformations (port-wine stains) and associated neurological findings, including seizures. On imaging, particularly head CT, Sturge-Weber syndrome is known to show prominent intraparenchymal white matter calcifications, especially in the areas of the brain that correspond to the affected vascular malformation. Given the context and the typical findings associated with this condition, the most likely finding on a head CT for this patient would be prominent intraparenchymal white matter calcification. Other options, such as intraparenchymal hemorrhage or subependymal giant cell astrocytoma, are less consistent with the presentation and known associations of Sturge-Weber syndrome. Therefore, the best-supported option is prominent intraparenchymal white matter calcification.
